PSE II · Chapter 24

Electric Potential

Energy, voltage & the scalar view of fields

← PSE II Course

24.0 — Energy Joins the Story

In Physics I, we discovered that energy methods often provide simpler solutions than force methods. Instead of tracking forces and accelerations through complex paths, we could use conservation of energy to relate initial and final states directly.

The same insight applies to electromagnetism. While Coulomb’s Law and Gauss’s Law give us the electric force and field, we can also develop an energy-based approach using electric potential energy and electric potential.

The concept of electric potential is intimately connected to our everyday experience with electricity. When we speak of a “12-volt battery” or a “120-volt outlet,” we are describing potential differences. The volt — named after Alessandro Volta (1745–1827), inventor of the first battery — measures electric potential.

“The language of experiment is more authoritative than any reasoning: facts can destroy our ratiocination — not vice versa.” — Alessandro Volta

Understanding electric potential answers the question posed in the chapter storyline: What exactly is a volt? By the end of this chapter, we’ll understand not only what a volt is, but why the potential difference in lightning strikes can reach hundreds of millions of volts — and why that makes lightning so dangerous.

Gravitational Analogy Preview

Gravitational System Electrical System
Gravitational potential energy \(U_{g} = mgh\) Electric potential energy \(U_{E}\)
Gravitational potential \(V_{g} = gh = U_{g}/m\) Electric potential \(V = U_{E}/q\)
\(g\) = gravitational field \(E\) = electric field
Mass \(m\) feels force \(\vec{F} = m\vec{g}\) Charge \(q\) feels force \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\)

*Just as gravitational potential (\(gh\)) is potential energy per unit mass, electric potential (\(V\)) is potential energy per unit charge. This analogy will guide our development throughout the chapter.

24.1 — Electric Potential Energy

Potential Energy in a Uniform Field

Recall from Physics I that potential energy is associated with conservative forces — forces for which the work done depends only on the initial and final positions, not on the path taken. The electric force is conservative because it depends only on position (like gravity) and satisfies curl conditions.

Consider a positive charge \(q\) in a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\) pointing in the \(- y\) direction (downward). If the charge moves from point A to point B through a displacement \(\vec{d}\), the work done by the electric field on the charge is:

\[W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = q\vec{E} \cdot \vec{d}\]

For a displacement in the direction of the field:

\[W = qEd\]

The change in electric potential energy is defined as the negative of this work:

\[\Delta U_{E} = - W = - qEd\]

This sign convention matches gravity: when an object falls, gravity does positive work and potential energy decreases.

Potential Energy of Point Charges

For two point charges \(q_{1}\) and \(q_{2}\) separated by distance \(r\), the electric potential energy of the system is:

\[U_{E} = k_{e}\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r}\]

Important features:

  • If both charges have the same sign: \(U_{E} > 0\) (positive work required to bring them together)
  • If charges have opposite signs: \(U_{E} < 0\) (negative work required — they attract)
  • \(U_{E} \rightarrow 0\) as \(r \rightarrow \infty\) (conventional reference point)

Comparison with Gravitational Potential Energy

Gravitational PE Electric PE
\(U_{g} = - G\frac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r}\) \(U_{E} = k_{e}\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r}\)
Always negative (masses attract) Can be positive or negative
Reference: \(U_{g} = 0\) at \(r = \infty\) Reference: \(U_{E} = 0\) at \(r = \infty\)

The key difference is the sign: gravitational forces are always attractive (negative PE), while electric forces can be attractive or repulsive.

Systems of Multiple Charges

For a system of multiple point charges, the total potential energy is the sum of potential energies for all pairs:

\[U_{E} = k_{e}\sum_{i < j}^{}\frac{q_{i}q_{j}}{r_{ij}}\]

For three charges:

\[U_{E} = k_{e}\left( \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}} + \frac{q_{1}q_{3}}{r_{13}} + \frac{q_{2}q_{3}}{r_{23}} \right)\]

Important: We count each pair once! The notation \(i < j\) ensures we don’t double-count.

24.2 — Electric Potential

Definition

Just as we defined the electric field as force per unit charge (\(\vec{E} = \vec{F}/q\)), we define electric potential as potential energy per unit charge:

\[V = \frac{U_{E}}{q}\]

The potential difference (or voltage) between points A and B is:

\[\Delta V = V_{B} - V_{A} = \frac{\Delta U_{E}}{q} = - \frac{W_{A \rightarrow B}}{q}\]

where \(W_{A \rightarrow B}\) is the work done by the electric field in moving charge \(q\) from A to B.

The Volt

The SI unit of electric potential is the volt (V):

\[1\ \text{V} = 1\ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{C}}\]

One volt means one joule of potential energy per coulomb of charge.

Important consequence: The electric field can be expressed in volts per meter:

\[1\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{C}} = 1\ \frac{\text{V}}{\text{m}}\]

This gives us a new interpretation of the electric field: E is the rate at which potential changes with position.

The Electron Volt

In atomic and nuclear physics, the joule is inconveniently large. The electron volt (eV) is defined as the energy gained by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt:

\[1\ \text{eV} = \left( 1.602 \times 10^{- 19}\ \text{C} \right)\left( 1\ \text{V} \right) = 1.602 \times 10^{- 19}\ \text{J}\]

Examples: - Visible light photons: 1.8 – 3.1 eV - Chemical bond energies: ~1 – 10 eV - Medical X-rays: ~10 – 100 keV - Nuclear binding energies: ~1 – 10 MeV

Potential vs. Potential Energy

Don’t confuse potential \(V\) with potential energy \(U_{E}\):

Electric Potential \(V\) Electric Potential Energy \(U_{E}\)
Property of the field (source charges) Property of a system (source + test charge)
Exists even without test charge Requires a test charge to exist
Scalar (units: volts) Scalar (units: joules)
\(V = U_{E}/q\) \(U_{E} = qV\)

Analogy: Electric potential is like the “height” in a gravitational field. A location has a definite height whether or not a mass is there. But gravitational PE requires both a height and a mass.

24.3 — Potential Difference in a Uniform Field

Basic Relationship

In a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\), the potential difference between two points A and B is:

\[V_{B} - V_{A} = - \int_{A}^{B}\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}\]

For a uniform field and a straight path:

\[\Delta V = - Ed\]

where \(d\) is the distance moved in the direction of the field.

Key insight: Electric potential decreases in the direction of the electric field. Field lines point from high potential to low potential — just as gravitational field lines point “downhill” from high gravitational potential to low.

Equipotential Surfaces

An equipotential surface is a surface on which all points have the same electric potential.

Properties of equipotential surfaces:

  1. No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential surface (since \(\Delta V = 0\), we have \(W = - q\Delta V = 0\))

  2. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to electric field lines

  3. Equipotential surfaces never cross each other

  4. The spacing of equipotential surfaces indicates field strength — closer spacing means stronger field

Uniform Field Equipotentials

In a uniform field, equipotential surfaces are parallel planes perpendicular to the field.

Example: Between parallel plate capacitor plates with potential difference \(\Delta V\) and separation \(d\):

\[E = \frac{\Delta V}{d}\]

If \(\Delta V = 12\) V and \(d = 0.30\) cm:

\[E = \frac{12\ \text{V}}{0.0030\ \text{m}} = 4000\ \text{V/m}\]

24.4 — Electric Potential Due to Point Charges

Single Point Charge

The electric potential at distance \(r\) from a point charge \(q\) is:

\[V = k_{e}\frac{q}{r}\]

Derivation: Starting from \(\Delta V = - \int\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}\) with \(\vec{E} = k_{e}q/r^{2}\ \hat{r}\) and taking the reference \(V = 0\) at \(r = \infty\):

\[V = - \int_{\infty}^{r}k_{e}\frac{q}{r\prime^{2}}dr\prime = k_{e}\frac{q}{r}\]

Key features:

  • \(V > 0\) for positive charge (potential hills)
  • \(V < 0\) for negative charge (potential wells)
  • \(V \rightarrow 0\) as \(r \rightarrow \infty\)
  • \(V \rightarrow \pm \infty\) as \(r \rightarrow 0\) (singularity at point charge location)

Multiple Point Charges

Because electric potential is a scalar, the total potential from multiple charges is simply the algebraic sum:

\[V = k_{e}\sum_{i}^{}\frac{q_{i}}{r_{i}}\]

No vector addition required! This is a major computational advantage of working with potential rather than field.

Example: Electric Dipole

An electric dipole consists of charges \(+ q\) and \(- q\) separated by distance \(2a\), located along the x-axis centered at the origin.

At point P on the y-axis at height \(y\):

Each charge is at distance \(r = \sqrt{a^{2} + y^{2}}\) from P.

\[V = k_{e}\frac{+ q}{r} + k_{e}\frac{- q}{r} = 0\]

The potential is zero everywhere on the perpendicular bisector of the dipole!

At point R on the positive x-axis at \(x > a\):

\[V = k_{e}\left( \frac{q}{x - a} + \frac{- q}{x + a} \right) = k_{e}q\frac{- 2a}{x^{2} - a^{2}}\]

For \(x \gg a\):

\[V \approx - \frac{2k_{e}qa}{x^{2}} = - \frac{k_{e}p}{x^{2}}\]

where \(p = 2qa\) is the dipole moment. The potential falls off as \(1/r^{2}\) far from a dipole (faster than \(1/r\) for a point charge).

24.5 — Obtaining Electric Field from Potential

The Gradient Relationship

The electric field and electric potential are intimately related. Given \(V\), we can find \(\vec{E}\):

\[\vec{E} = - \nabla V = - \left( \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} + \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k} \right)\]

In one dimension:

\[E_{x} = - \frac{dV}{dx}\]

Physical interpretation: The electric field points in the direction of steepest decrease of potential, with magnitude equal to the rate of decrease.

Graphical Interpretation

If you have a graph of \(V\) vs. \(x\):

  • The slope at any point gives \(-E_{x}\)
  • Steeper slopes mean stronger fields
  • Where \(V\) is flat (slope \(=0\)), the field is zero

Example: Checking the Point Charge Result

For a point charge: \(V = k_{e}q/r\)

In spherical coordinates:

\[E_{r} = - \frac{dV}{dr} = - \frac{d}{dr}\left( k_{e}\frac{q}{r} \right) = k_{e}\frac{q}{r^{2}}\]

This matches Coulomb’s Law! The derivative method gives the same result as direct application of Coulomb’s Law.

Why Use Potential?

Since \(\vec{E}\) and \(V\) contain the same information, why work with potential?

  1. Scalars are simpler. Adding potentials is easier than adding vectors.

  2. Energy calculations are direct. \(\Delta U_{E} = q\Delta V\) — no integration needed once you have \(V\).

  3. Experimental accessibility. Voltmeters directly measure potential differences.

  4. Connection to circuits. Circuit analysis is built on voltage (potential difference).

24.6 — Electric Potential Due to Continuous Charge Distributions

For continuous charge distributions, we integrate:

\[V = k_{e}\int\frac{dq}{r}\]

This is often easier than the corresponding integral for \(\vec{E}\) because:

  • \(V\) is a scalar — no components to track
  • No direction cosines or unit vectors needed

Example: Uniformly Charged Ring

A ring of radius \(a\) carries total charge \(Q\). Find the potential at point P on the axis, distance \(x\) from the center.

Setup: Every element \(dq\) is the same distance \(r = \sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}}\) from P.

\[V = k_{e}\int\frac{dq}{\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}}} = \frac{k_{e}}{\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}}}\int dq = \frac{k_{e}Q}{\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}}}\]

Finding the field: Using \(E_{x} = - dV/dx\):

\[E_{x} = - \frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{k_{e}Q}{\sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}}} \right) = \frac{k_{e}Qx}{\left( a^{2} + x^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\]

This matches our Chapter 23 result from direct integration!

Example: Uniformly Charged Disk

A disk of radius \(R\) has uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\). Find the potential on the axis at distance \(x\) from the center.

Strategy: Build the disk from rings of radius \(r\), thickness \(dr\):

\[dq = \sigma\left( 2\pi r\, dr \right)\]

Each ring contributes:

\[dV = \frac{k_{e}\left( 2\pi\sigma r\, dr \right)}{\sqrt{r^{2} + x^{2}}}\]

Integrating:

\[V = 2\pi k_{e}\sigma\int_{0}^{R}\frac{r\, dr}{\sqrt{r^{2} + x^{2}}} = 2\pi k_{e}\sigma\left\lbrack \sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}} - x \right\rbrack\]

Or equivalently:

\[V = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\left( \sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}} - x \right)\]

Example: Finite Line of Charge

A rod of length \(\ell\) carries total charge \(Q\) with uniform linear charge density \(\lambda = Q/\ell\). Find the potential at point P located distance \(a\) above one end.

Setup: Let the rod lie along the x-axis from \(x = 0\) to \(x = \ell\), with P at the origin of the y-axis at height \(a\).

\[r = \sqrt{x^{2} + a^{2}}\]

\[V = k_{e}\int_{0}^{\ell}\frac{\lambda\, dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} + a^{2}}}\]

Using the standard integral \(\int dx/\sqrt{x^{2} + a^{2}} = \ln\left( x + \sqrt{x^{2} + a^{2}} \right)\):

\[V = k_{e}\lambda\left\lbrack \ln\left( \ell + \sqrt{\ell^{2} + a^{2}} \right) - \ln\left( a \right) \right\rbrack\]

\[V = k_{e}\frac{Q}{\ell}\ln\left( \frac{\ell + \sqrt{\ell^{2} + a^{2}}}{a} \right)\]

Limiting case: When \(a \gg \ell\), series expansion gives \(V \approx k_{e}Q/a\) — the potential of a point charge, as expected.

24.7 — Potential of a Charged Conductor

Conductors are Equipotentials

Because \(\vec{E} = 0\) inside a conductor in equilibrium (Chapter 23), and \(\vec{E} = - \nabla V\), the potential must be constant throughout a conductor.

Every point on and inside a conductor has the same potential.

This has important practical implications:

  • The entire surface of a conductor is an equipotential surface
  • Field lines meet conductor surfaces perpendicularly
  • Charge redistributes itself to maintain constant potential

Potential of a Charged Sphere

A conducting sphere of radius \(R\) carrying total charge \(Q\):

Outside the sphere (\(r > R\)):

\[V = \frac{k_{e}Q}{r}\]

On the surface and inside (\(r \leq R\)):

\[V = \frac{k_{e}Q}{R} = \text{constant}\]

The potential is continuous at \(r = R\), but notice:

  • \(V\) is constant inside (flat)
  • \(V\) decreases as \(1/r\) outside

The electric field is the negative derivative:

  • Inside: \(E = 0\) (as expected)
  • Outside: \(E = k_{e}Q/r^{2}\) (point-charge behavior)

Sharp Points on Conductors

On an irregularly shaped conductor, charge accumulates at regions of high curvature (sharp points). This creates high surface charge density \(\sigma\) and high electric field \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_{0}\) near the points.

Applications:

  • Lightning rods: sharp points create intense fields that ionize air
  • Van de Graaff generators: smooth dome minimizes corona discharge
  • Corona discharge: visible glow at sharp points due to ionized air

24.8 — Energy Stored in the Electric Field

When we assemble a system of charges, work must be done against (or by) electric forces. This work is stored as electric potential energy.

Energy of Two Point Charges

To bring charge \(q_{2}\) from infinity to distance \(r\) from charge \(q_{1}\):

\[U_{E} = q_{2}V_{1} = q_{2} \cdot k_{e}\frac{q_{1}}{r} = k_{e}\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r}\]

Energy of Three Charges

For three charges at the vertices of a triangle:

\[U_{E} = k_{e}\left( \frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{12}} + \frac{q_{1}q_{3}}{r_{13}} + \frac{q_{2}q_{3}}{r_{23}} \right)\]

The energy can be positive (work required to assemble) or negative (energy released).

Application: Motion of Charged Particles

Conservation of energy provides a powerful tool for analyzing charged particle motion:

\[K_{i} + U_{i} = K_{f} + U_{f}\]

\[\frac{1}{2}mv_{i}^{2} + qV_{i} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{f}^{2} + qV_{f}\]

Example: A proton is released from rest near the positive plate of a parallel plate capacitor with \(\Delta V = 100\) V. Find its speed when it reaches the negative plate.

Using energy conservation:

\[0 + qV_{i} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{f}^{2} + qV_{f}\]

\[q\left( V_{i} - V_{f} \right) = \frac{1}{2}mv_{f}^{2}\]

\[q\Delta V = \frac{1}{2}mv_{f}^{2}\]

\[v_{f} = \sqrt{\frac{2q\Delta V}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\left( 1.602 \times 10^{- 19} \right)\left( 100 \right)}{1.673 \times 10^{- 27}}}\]

\[v_{f} = 1.38 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m/s}\]

24.9 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Electric potential \(V\) is potential energy per unit charge: \(V = U_{E}/q\)

  2. Potential difference (voltage) between two points: \(\Delta V = - \int\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}\)

  3. The volt is defined as 1 joule per coulomb: 1 V = 1 J/C

  4. Electric field points from high to low potential (like “downhill”)

  5. Equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines

  6. Potential due to a point charge: \(V = k_{e}q/r\)

  7. For multiple charges, add potentials algebraically (scalar addition)

  8. Electric field from potential: \(\vec{E} = - \nabla V\)

  9. A conductor in equilibrium is an equipotential

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Electric potential energy (point charges) \(U_{E} = k_{e}\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r}\)
Electric potential (definition) \(V = \frac{U_{E}}{q}\)
Potential difference \(\Delta V = V_{B} - V_{A} = - \int_{A}^{B}\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}\)
Potential (point charge) \(V = k_{e}\frac{q}{r}\)
Potential (multiple charges) \(V = k_{e}\sum_{i}^{}\frac{q_{i}}{r_{i}}\)
Potential (continuous distribution) \(V = k_{e}\int\frac{dq}{r}\)
Field from potential \(\vec{E} = - \nabla V = - \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}\hat{i} - \frac{\partial V}{\partial y}\hat{j} - \frac{\partial V}{\partial z}\hat{k}\)
Uniform field \(\Delta V = - Ed\)
Energy conservation \(K_{i} + qV_{i} = K_{f} + qV_{f}\)
Electron volt \(1\ \text{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{- 19}\ \text{J}\)

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 25, we will study capacitance — the ability of a system of conductors to store charge and energy. Capacitors are fundamental components in electrical circuits, storing energy in the electric field between their plates.

The relationship between charge, potential, and capacitance will be:

\[C = \frac{Q}{\Delta V}\]

We will find that the energy stored in a capacitor can be expressed as \(U = \frac{1}{2}CV^{2}\), or equivalently as energy stored in the electric field itself with an energy density \(u = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_{0}E^{2}\).

*The development from Coulomb’s Law through Gauss’s Law to Electric Potential represents three complementary ways of describing electrostatic phenomena: forces, fields, and energy. Each perspective offers different insights and computational advantages. The skilled physicist knows when to use each approach — and that wisdom comes from practice!
